It boots… / X Post Log in Sign up Post Log in Sign up Alexey Fateev on X: "I deleted Linux completely, baked Qwen3-0.6B into a 24 KB pure x86-64 assembly OS, and it runs up to 54% faster than native Linux llama.cpp. The entire Multiboot OS binary (asm-llm-os.elf) is 24,252 bytes, written from scratch without Linux, Windows, C, Rust, or libc. It boots in 74 to 94 ms straight into 64-bit Long Mode, wakes every CPU core over APIC, maps the 614 MiB Q8_0 weights directly from physical RAM, and drops you into a live multi-turn KV-cache chat over VGA, PS/2 keyboard, and serial. I ran head-to-head CPU benchmarks against llama.cpp (Q8_0, -ngl 0) on the same AMD EPYC 7642: - 1 thread hits 23.67 tok/s vs 16.63 (+42%) - 4 threads hit 78.89 tok/s vs 51.08 (+54%) - 8 threads hit 118.08 tok/s vs 80.79 (+46%) - 16 threads hit 134.94 tok/s vs 103.03 (+31%, 136.6 peak) On a diskless 0 GB Proxmox VM (2014 12-core Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3, 2 GiB RAM), it boots straight to the prompt in under 5 seconds (95 ms kernel boot) and runs live out of RAM at 78 tok/s decode and up to 111.5 tok/s prefill, with a hybrid BIOS+UEFI ISO builder included too. Output stays bit-exact across thread counts and matches all 64 greedy tokens against PyTorch FP32 (0.99965 cosine). The 14.7 KB Linux ELF build (FAST_Q8=1 INT8xINT8 AVX2+F16C) also beats llama.cpp by 18% to 36% from 1 to 40 threads, and booting bare metal with 2 MiB huge pages squeezes out another 10% on top. story|title:amd and intel s ai compute e.content_excerpt: The rival chipmakers' joint ACEv1 specification promises 16x matrix compute density over existing instructions, with hardware support expected no earlier than 2028 AMD and Intel, two companies that have spent decades trying to eat each other’s lunch, just co-authored the recipe. Their shared AI Compute Extensions specification, known as ACEv1, has been merged into the GCC 17 development branch as of September 2, 2026, bringing standardized AI acceleration capabilities to the world’s most widely used open-source compiler toolchain. The move represents a rare moment of genuine technical cooperation between the x86 duopoly, and it carries implications well beyond compiler flags. In a computing landscape increasingly dominated by Arm-based designs and purpose-built AI accelerators, AMD and Intel are betting that a unified approach to matrix computation can keep the x86 architecture relevant for the next decade of AI workloads. At its core, ACEv1 introduces a matrix acceleration architecture optimized for AI and machine learning tasks. The specification uses outer-product instructions to deliver up to 16 times the compute density compared to equivalent AVX10 operations. The standard supports a range of low-precision numerical formats including INT8, FP8, and BF16. These formats matter because most AI inference workloads don’t need the full precision of traditional floating-point math. ACEv1 builds on concepts from Intel’s Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX), which shipped in the company’s Sapphire Rapids server chips. But there’s a crucial distinction: ACEv1 is not backward-compatible with AMX. The specification was first published in June 2026 through the x86 Ecosystem Advisory Group, an industry body that AMD and Intel formed in 2024 specifically to tackle standardization challenges. Engineers from both companies contributed the compiler patches that landed in GCC 17’s development branch on September 2. Full GCC support is expected to arrive with the GCC 17.1 release, projected for March to April 2027. No hardware implementing ACEv1 is anticipated before 2028, with AMD hinting that these AI features could appear in its upcoming Zen 7 processor architecture. The lack of backward compatibility with Intel’s AMX signals that both companies decided a fresh start was more valuable than preserving legacy code paths. For software developers who built around AMX, this means migration work ahead. For the broader ecosystem, it means a single target to optimize for, regardl

story|title:building a better dependabot.content_excerpt: dependabot · renovate · dependency management · ai agents · cloudflare workers · durable objects · github Felix was built with a lot of help from Claude Code, and I used an LLM to help organize this post. The opinions (and the grudges against Dependabot) are my own. Here are two pull requests for the same Rust upgrade on my Rust template repository. Dependabot’s bumped the rust image in the Dockerfile but not rust-toolchain.toml alongside it. The other one bumped both pins together, explained why it didn’t touch the rust-version MSRV in Cargo.toml , and listed what changed upstream in 1.100 that could affect the repo. That one came from Felix. Dependabot promised to automate away a chore many of us skipped because of the tedious, never-ending onslaught of updates, and when it launched, people loved it. Years later, I have a bad case of what I call dependency burnout. Dependabot bumps something, the build breaks, and now fixing it is my problem. Multiply that across every repo and I just stopped merging them altogether unless I needed a bugfix or a new feature. Meanwhile, the steady stream of new CVEs and zero-days has made keeping dependencies up to date more important than ever. And Dependabot hasn’t really kept up. The alternatives don’t always fare better in practice, either. At my $DAYJOB we use Renovate , but it’s been dialed way back. It only runs once a week and the rebase commands are turned off, so its PRs go stale and start conflicting before anyone gets to them. So I built Felix. The name is a nod to Fix-It Felix Jr. from Wreck-It Ralph , because the whole point is that it fixes things, and doesn’t just bump numbers and walk away. Dependabot, Renovate, and the rest of the update bots are rigid in their approach. Find all the Cargo.toml , package.json , requirements.txt and lockfiles, check upstream for new versions, and if anything changed, update the manifest and lockfile and open a pull request. This is exactly the kind of work agents are great at. It’s tedious, it’s well defined, and verifying it is just running the build and tests. Felix still does the boring deterministic parts the old way. Versions come from a registry lookup, never from the model, so it won’t invent a tag that doesn’t exist. Then an agent takes over: it consults the release notes, makes the code changes, and looks for everything outside the dependency files that also needs to move. story|title:estimating llm decode speed.content_excerpt: A per-operation model calibrated on public benchmarks, corrected for concurrent sessions with measured runs, and checked on machines it never saw Build Finder lists every hardware build that runs a chosen open-weight language model at a target decode speed, cheapest per token per second (tok/s) first: the price of the whole build divided by its speed. Its catalog holds 273 GPUs, used as 1 to 8 cards, 619 CPUs and 333 complete systems, at dated US prices. Speeds come from a per-operation model: each operation of a token's pass takes the longer of reading its bytes and doing its arithmetic, at efficiencies and engine costs fitted per engine and hardware family to 424 one-session benchmarks from 120 devices. For several sessions at once, a correction with two parameters per engine, model kind and session range is fitted to 418 measured runs on 19 machines. Against the 427 measured decode runs the page lists without speculative decoding, the median estimate is 11% below the measured speed on NVIDIA hardware (385 runs), 1.43 times the measured speed on Macs (31 runs) and 1.73 times the measured speed on Inkling 2 Mini (11 runs). On the GeForce RTX 3090, which neither fit has seen on llama.cpp (CUDA), 87% of 54 runs fall within 1.25 times the measured speed and 100% within 1.5 times. Runs with speculative decoding, which the estimates leave out, measured a median 2.3 times the estimate. We describe the data, the model, the fit, its validation and what the estimates cannot yet capture. Running an open-weight model on one's own hardware starts with a buying question: which machine gives the decode speed a use needs, and what does it cost? The evidence people find is scattered across benchmark threads, engine READMEs and forum posts, each for one card, one engine, one model file and usually one session, often without the details needed to compare them, while prices move every week. Build Finder answers the question for every build in its catalog at once. A user picks a model, the tokens per second each session should get, the most they would pay per tok/s and how many sessions run at once. The page lists every measured build that matches and every build the model expects to meet the target, cheapest first, with the price of the whole machine. This paper explains where each number on that page comes from, and how far it can be trusted. story|title:llm asm pure x86 64 assembly.content_excerpt: Qwen3-0.6B inference (12 KB), bare-metal bootable OS (22 KB), and from-scratch Mini-GPT trainer with live Braille TUI (32 KB) in 100% pure x86-64 NASM assembly. Zero C, zero libc, zero dependencies. Three complete LLM projects written in 100% pure x86-64 NASM assembly. Zero C, zero C++, zero Rust, zero libc, zero libm, zero runtime dependencies. Assembled directly with nasm and linked with ld . Every math kernel ( expf , sincosf , RMSNorm , RoPE , SiLU , Softmax ), AVX2+FMA+F16C GEMM/GEMV engine, BPE tokenizer, clone() / futex() thread pool, bare-metal SMP kernel, analytical backward pass, AdamW optimizer, and live Unicode Braille TUI is hand-written x86-64 assembly ( 17,252 lines total across all three projects). Measured on the same machine ( AMD EPYC 7642 , 47C online, 256 MiB L3, DDR4, CPU-only -ngl 0 ), same model ( Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0 : 613.66 MiB .asmbin v2 FP16-scale vs 604.15 MiB GGUF Q8_0 ), 34 prompt tokens / 64 generated tokens, 3 -run average: (Note: llama.cpp uses batched GEMM for prompt prefill pp34 , whereas llm.asm runs token-by-token GEMV. For autoregressive decode tg64 , llm.asm ( FAST_Q8=1 ) combines INT8xINT8 AVX2 vpmaddubsw / vpmaddwd , .asmbin v2 FP16 block scales ( F16C vcvtph2ps ), monotonic next-row prefetch, contiguous head-major KV-cache, and parallel GQA attention — beating llama.cpp by +18%..+36% across 1..40 threads while producing bit-exact deterministic outputs across all thread counts. The bare-metal OS gains another ~10% from 2 MiB huge-page identity mapping.) Full step-by-step setup, model download, CLI flags, and benchmarks: 01-qwen3-inference/README.md . Full QEMU KVM, bootable ISO, and 0 GB disk Proxmox VE deployment guide: 02-baremetal-os/README.md . Full training, live Braille TUI, checkpoint chat loop, and PyTorch gradient check guide: 03-minigpt-train/README.md . Full architecture, QEMU nested-SVM + VNC demo, SFT/GRPO training, and KVM verifier guide: 04-ring1-kernel-surgeon/README.md . Every phase is built on the same engineering rules: no runtime libraries, deterministic parallel partitioning, and numerical verification against independent Python/PyTorch references. See each project's README for full tables, memory layouts, and reproduction steps: Qwen3-0.6B inference (12 KB), bare-metal bootable OS (22 KB), and from-scratch Mini-GPT trainer with live Braille TUI (32 KB) in 100% pure x86-64 NASM assembly. story|title:show me a coding agent skill.content_excerpt: agents got more intelligent on paper, but the experience of using them got noticeably worse along this dimension. the thing people used to love about claude - its voice, it's personality, its "soul" has been flushed out in the RL dungeon sol is somewhat less cringe but still regularly hits us with walls of jargon that make eyes glaze over We've been playing with internal tools to make this better, specifically for coding, and publishing them in a skill we call show-me . It's live in humanlayer today, and if you want it in any other coding agent - you can get it here: If you ever watched coda hale's talk on intuition vs. attention in infrastructure systems , it's somewhat inspired: Just as an axe must fit the human hand to be useful, software must fit the human mind to be useful /show-me prompts the agent to use concise visuals to explain what's happening, instead of walls of prose. This is really good for program design - the phase many folks skip these days, but that I think is essential. You should be discussing the shape of the code (the types, the signatures, the call stacks) before agents get to work on writing it. The same techniques can also be used to explore large diffs post-hoc to understand what to dig into during review. Same idea on the frontend, with the state hooks and module boundaries that matter kept in and everything else left out. For orchestration or control-flow work, or just any backend-shaped problem, dillon gave us this "call stack" shape. A classic. If your chat interface supports inline mermaid, these can help a lot. (Sometimes they're still slop, but it's usually better than reading words) A shallow file tree, one line of responsibility per entry. Good for "where does this live" and for scoping a refactor. The shape of the code before any of it exists - the stuff that's too internal for an architecture doc but that an agent can still get wrong. And for a state or control-flow change, where the shape is pseudocode rather than real code: HTML has replaced figma for a lot of our prototyping work. (tbh i never really was super handy with figma anyway) I also wanna hat tip Matt Pocock for the html explainers that are generated by his /teach skill - very good. After installing the skill, invoke /show-me or ask the agent to use the show-me skill. Point it at a route, service, feature, pull request, or current topic, or just use it to ask the model to restate a question or statement. Let us know what you think! Tag @humanlayer_dev or @d

story|title:the agent tax has arrived go.content_excerpt: Google has announced some major changes to their Google Workspace (Gmail, Google Docs and all related apps) pricing, as part of their new MCP rollout. I think this is the first major product that's attempting to tax agentic use cases. I'm not sure it will work. Effectively two things. Firstly, all agents need to use MCP, not API to interact with Google. Quite how they plan on enforcing this I'm not sure, as the best I suspect they can do is behavioural profiling of what APIs get called, which seems to be quite difficult. I strongly believe this is mostly targeted at large AI companies and not smaller developers or solo users; but it is likely to have serious impact on any company that is (or will) start integrating agentic workflows into their products. Secondly, a new pricing tier for said MCPs. In true Google style it's complicated, but in essence it's a charge per 1000 requests , with different types of requests using different pricing tiers. Roughly speaking, you can read 1000 emails via MCP for $0.20. There is a free tier of 5,000 calls a day, but this is grouped across all access for a specific Google Cloud project. Probably fine for solo use or a smaller business's internal agentic tooling, but past that it is going to be a major issue. There is an enormous difference in the allowances for "legacy" applications using the REST API vs the new tiers for MCP. On the REST API, each user of the API gets its own allowance. On the free tier for REST, each user can do 6,000 quota units per minute of requests. This roughly equates to reading 100 emails a minute, per user . There is another project level cap of 20,000 emails a minute. Previously going above this required a quota request but wasn't charged for. Now you have to move to the paid tier to go higher, but even there a REST app gets a huge free daily allowance - 10 million email reads a day - before it pays anything. MCP on the paid tier gets none. So the real way to look at this is that if you are building a REST API you can read 20,000 emails a minute for free, but if you are building some agentic tooling you can read 5,000 emails a day for free, and if you need more than that you get charged around $0.20 per thousand for every email you read, including the first 5,000. It's an enormous difference, and puts the Google Maps pricing changes of yore to shame in scale. story|title:what it takes to let ai agen.content_excerpt: Letting AI agents work unattended is safe when the rules are set up before you leave. A practical look at planning, sandboxing, testing and reviewing their work. The concern is warranted. There are plenty of stories of AI building fragile software with glaring security holes . Agents have also made reckless decisions on their own, like dropping a production database . It’s sensible to be wary, but don’t dismiss the idea. With the right guardrails and practices in place, you can safely hand work to agents and step away while they do it, shipping high-quality software at a much faster pace. Even in security-sensitive environments, the same approach applies, although you need to be deliberate about where the agent runs and what code leaves your network. The catch is that the effort doesn’t disappear with asynchronous agents. It shifts to planning before the agent starts and reviewing what it produces. In this article, I’ll cover what it takes to work with asynchronous agents safely and get quality output from them. I won’t compare particular tools or models, since these advance quickly. Instead, I’ll focus on concepts and practices that apply regardless of harness (the tool that runs the agent) and model. Any tools I do mention are just examples I’ve used myself. Most developers started out using AI for coding in a chat window, either in the browser or as a side panel in their IDE. When these chat tools first arrived, they were mind-blowing. AI agents, though, are so much more than a simple chat interface. An agent can read context, make decisions, and take actions on your behalf, like writing code or debugging an application. How you work with an agent can be synchronous or asynchronous. In a synchronous setup, you watch the agent work in real time, answering its questions and steering it as it goes. In an asynchronous setup, you hand it a task and walk away. You come back to a pull request that’s ready for review. Removing that hands-on control lets you scale your effort by running multiple agents in parallel, so you can get through far more work in the same amount of time. Working asynchronously changes what the quality of the resulting code depends on. When you work synchronously, you’re the safety net. You notice the agent drifting, correct it mid-task, and catch mistakes as they happen.
